name: Abu Dhabi
summary: Operating as the Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), this jurisdiction uses the direct application of English common law and provides a flexible, risk-based captive framework. It offers a dedicated rulebook and a streamlined application process with four distinct classes of captive insurers to meet varied business needs. A major benefit is the 0% tax environment guaranteed until 2065, along with the ability to outsource all management functions to ADGM-authorized managers.
tax_notes: 0% tax until 2065; 5% VAT may apply

name: Alabama
summary: Alabama positions itself at the forefront of the industry by offering innovative features like a 60-day provisional license and the ability to form as any entity allowed under law, including Series LLCs. Legislation enacted in 2006 was significantly updated in 2016 to modernize the Alabama Captive Act and enhance competitiveness. The state is active in advocacy through the Alabama Captive Insurance Association and offers prorated premium taxes in the first year.
tax_notes: $100,000 maximum cap; no tax on dormant captives

name: Alberta
summary: Alberta enacted dedicated captive insurance legislation under the Captive Insurance Companies Act (SA 2021, c. C-2.4), which came into force on July 1, 2022, making it the second Canadian province with a standalone captive statute. Administered by the Alberta Superintendent of Insurance (Treasury Board and Finance), the regime authorizes pure, association, and sophisticated insured captives—formed as either corporations or limited partnerships—as well as redomestication of foreign captives. Driven by strong demand from the energy, natural resource, and commercial sectors, along with Canada's lowest provincial corporate income tax rate (8%) and streamlined 6-week licensing, Alberta has rapidly expanded its captive insurance sector.
legislation: Captive Insurance Companies Act, SA 2021, c. C-2.4 (in force July 1, 2022) & Captive Insurance Companies Regulation, Alta. Reg. 100/2022
applicable_legislation: Captive Insurance Companies Act (SA 2021, c. C-2.4); Captive Insurance Companies Regulation (Alta. Reg. 100/2022); Captive Insurance Companies (Prescribed Enactments) Regulation (Alta. Reg. 103/2022); Fees Under the Captive Insurance Companies Act Order (Ministerial Order 14/2022); Classes of Insurance Regulation (Alta. Reg. 144/2011); Recovery of Insurance Administration Costs Regulation (Alta. Reg. 102/2022); Insurance Enforcement and Administration Regulation (Alta. Reg. 101/2022); Business Corporations Act (RSA 2000, c. B-9); Partnership Act (RSA 2000, c. P-3); Alberta Corporate Tax Act (RSA 2000, c. A-15).

min_capital.Pure Captive: CAD 250,000 minimum base capital (or greater of 20% of first CAD 5M Net Insurance Revenue + 10% over CAD 5M, or 15% of net Liabilities for Incurred Claims for P&C; subject to Superintendent's risk-based determination)
min_capital.Association Captive: CAD 500,000 minimum base capital (or greater of formulaic revenue/claims thresholds or actuary-proposed risk-based amount; subject to Superintendent's determination)
min_capital.Sophisticated Insured Captive: CAD 500,000 minimum base capital (insureds must demonstrate insurance expertise and pay at least CAD 500,000 in aggregate annual premiums; subject to Superintendent's determination)

tax_notes: Subject to federal and provincial corporate income tax (8% Alberta general corporate tax rate) and Alberta insurance premiums tax under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (3% on life, accident and sickness insurance; 4% on property, casualty and other insurance contracts on Alberta risks).
contact_name: Erin O'Neill, Alberta Superintendent of Insurance

fees.licensing_incorporation: CAD 500 document filing fee (for association/sophisticated insured filings under s. 15) plus licence fee per class of insurance: CAD 600 each for Life, Property, Accident & Sickness, or Hail insurance; CAD 100 for one or more of any other class (50% prorated if issued after 8 months of the licensing year, per Ministerial Order 14/2022).
fees.annual_fees: Annual licence renewal fee (due by November 30 via IRIS): CAD 600 each for Life, Property, Accident & Sickness, or Hail insurance; CAD 100 for one or more of any other class; CAD 600 for run-off/discontinued renewal; plus annual regulatory cost recovery assessment under the Recovery of Insurance Administration Costs Regulation.
fees.premium_tax_rate: 3% on life, accident and sickness insurance premiums; 4% on property and casualty and all other insurance contracts on risks insured in Alberta (under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act). 8% provincial corporate income tax rate.

annual_filing_requirements: Electronic filing via IRIS required: Captive Annual Return Template and Signed Affidavit within 60 days after calendar year-end; Consolidated Audited Financial Statements (under IFRS 17), Auditor's Report, and Appointed Actuary's Report within 180 days after fiscal year-end; Alberta Premium Tax Return by May 15; Annual Licence Renewal by November 30; monthly Anti-Terrorism Financing Report by the 15th of each month. Principal place of business and records must be maintained in Alberta.

captive_administrator.name: Erin O'Neill, Alberta Superintendent of Insurance

regulator.name: Office of the Alberta Superintendent of Insurance, Alberta Treasury Board and Finance
regulator.address: 402 Terrace Building, 9515 - 107 Street NW, Edmonton, Alberta T5K 2C3

name: Anguilla
summary: Anguilla's Insurance Act provides a comprehensive framework for domestic, offshore, and captive insurance, notably including a specific 2018 provision for producer-affiliated reinsurance companies. The domicile offers five sub-categories of Class B licenses, ranging from unrestricted foreign business to single-owner captives. Unless maintaining a permanent local staff, insurers are required to appoint a licensed insurance manager.
tax_notes: Tax-neutral structures for Class B insurers

name: Arizona
summary: Established in 2002, Arizona is a mature and proven domicile supported by a stable regulatory team and a well-established network of local service providers. The state is highly competitive due to the absence of insurance premium taxes and state/local income taxes for most licensed captives. It provides an electronic filing portal and a cost-effective application process, licensing varied structures including agency and branch captives.
tax_notes: No premium or state income taxes; flat annual license fee

name: Arkansas
summary: Arkansas aggressively recruits captives by refining its laws, including major changes in 2017 and 2019 that reduced capital requirements and welcomed RRGs. It is recognized as one of the most cost-effective domiciles, featuring low application and license fees and a $100,000 tax liability cap. The Arkansas Insurance Department offers no-cost preliminary analyses for companies considering captive formation.
tax_notes: $100,000 maximum annual tax liability

name: Aruba
summary: Aruba offers a safe and stable environment for financial services with an international legal framework overseen by the Central Bank of Aruba. Captives are defined as businesses insuring risks originating almost exclusively from shareholders, affiliates, or joint venture participants. Operations must maintain an office in Aruba for financial administration and have at least one managing director residing on the island.

min_capital.General: Subject to Central Bank review and actuarial report

tax_notes: Requires annual audited financial statements

name: Bahrain
summary: Bahrain serves as a regional base for international insurers, with a sector regulated by the Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB) as a single regulator since 2002. The CBB differentiates between captive and commercial insurers, offering lower capital and solvency requirements for captives provided they do not include third-party liability risks. The domicile is supported by a large pool of brokers, actuaries, and insurance managers.

min_capital.Captive: Risk-based; lower than traditional insurers unless third-party liability is involved

tax_notes: Competitive regulatory environment

name: Barbados
summary: Barbados is a top-tier domicile known for its political stability and extensive bilateral double taxation treaty network with countries like Canada and the US. In 2019, it eliminated its ring-fenced regime, replacing the Exempt Insurance Act with a unified Insurance Act classified into three distinct license classes. Class 1 captives are restricted to related party business, while Class 2 can underwrite third-party risks with a 2% tax rate.
tax_notes: 0% for Class 1; 2% for Class 2 and Class 3 entities

fees.annual_fees: 2019-0.03% of total assets or minimum of $30,000 BDS; 2020-0.04% of total assets or minimum of $40,000 BDS; 2021-0.05% of total assets or minimum of $50,000 BDS
fees.premium_tax_rate: Class 1: none; Class 2: 2% on first $250k taxable income; Class 3: 2% (intermediaries, managers, holdings). Special FET exemption (1-4%) if Barbados-domiciled.

applicable_legislation: Exempt Insurance Act CAP. 308A; Insurance Act CAP. 310; Financial Services Commission Act, 2010-21.

regulator.name: Financial Services Commission
regulator.address: Harbour Industrial Park, Building 4, Suites 301 & 302, St. Michael, BB11142

name: Bermuda
summary: Bermuda is a global authority in the captive market, reaching full Solvency II equivalence in 2016 following oversight by the Bermuda Monetary Authority (BMA). Captives benefit from a robust market that provides open-market underwriting capacity not easily found elsewhere. As a reciprocal jurisdiction under the NAIC, Bermuda-based insurers can operate in the US without additional capital requirements.
tax_notes: Tax-competitive environment

fees.licensing_incorporation: Class 1: $2,250; Class 2: $4,375; Class 3: $17,800 minimum - based on GWP
fees.annual_fees: Class 1: $2,250; Class 2: $4,375; Class 3: $17,800 minimum - based on GWP

applicable_legislation: The primary legislation relating to insurance business is the Insurance Act 1978, as amended, and related regulations.

name: British Columbia
summary: British Columbia enacted Canada's first dedicated captive insurance statute in 1987 under the Insurance (Captive Company) Act (RSBC 1996, c. 227) and remains one of two Canadian provinces with standalone captive legislation alongside Alberta. Regulated by the BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA), which succeeded the Financial Institutions Commission (FICOM) in 2019, it permits pure, association, and sophisticated insured captives—the latter requiring insureds to have aggregate annual insurance premiums of at least CAD 500,000. Captives can write nearly all classes of insurance or reinsurance (excluding direct surety and non-fleet automobile) and require a minimum of CAD 200,000 in shareholders' equity and CAD 100,000 in reserves.
legislation: Insurance (Captive Company) Act, RSBC 1996, c. 227 & Insurance (Captive Company) Regulation, BC Reg. 99/2017
applicable_legislation: Insurance (Captive Company) Act, RSBC 1996, c. 227; Insurance (Captive Company) Regulation, BC Reg. 99/2017 (as amended by BC Reg. 183/2024); Financial Institutions Act, RSBC 1996, c. 141; Financial Services Authority Act, SBC 2019, c. 14; Insurance Act, RSBC 2012, c. 1; Business Corporations Act, SBC 2002, c. 57; Insurance Premium Tax Act, RSBC 1996, c. 232.

min_capital.Pure, Association, & Sophisticated Insur: CAD 300,000 combined minimum (at least CAD 200,000 shareholders' equity and CAD 100,000 reserves per s. 8 of ICCA and s. 5 of BC Reg. 99/2017, or such higher amount as the Superintendent requires to maintain solvency)

tax_notes: Subject to BC Insurance Premium Tax on BC risks (4.4% property and fleet auto, 4% general/other, 2% life, accident and sickness) and federal (15%) and provincial (12%) corporate income taxes.
contact_name: Tolga Yalkin, CEO & Superintendent of Financial Institutions

fees.licensing_incorporation: CAD 10,000 application fee for initial registration (effective September 1, 2024 under BC Reg. 183/2024; previously CAD 3,000).
fees.annual_fees: Variable based on non-consolidated assets plus 0.019% of prior fiscal year written premiums (effective September 1, 2024): assets <= CAD 100M: CAD 5,000 + 0.019% of written premiums; assets > CAD 100M to CAD 1B: CAD 7,500 + 0.019% of written premiums; assets > CAD 1B: CAD 10,000 + 0.019% of written premiums. Consent fees: CAD 5,000 amalgamation, CAD 500 change in control, CAD 100 articles amendment.
fees.premium_tax_rate: BC Insurance Premium Tax on taxable BC premiums: 4.4% for property and automobile insurance; 4% for general/other insurance; 2% for life, accident and sickness, and loss-of-wages insurance. Corporate income tax rates: 15% federal, 12% provincial.

annual_filing_requirements: Registration expires 90 days after fiscal year-end and must be renewed annually via BCFSA's IRIS portal on or before 90 days after fiscal year-end, including: renewal application and fee, Captive Insurance Financial Schedule, audited financial statements (prepared under IFRS 17) with auditor's report, independent actuarial report (FCIA), parent/association financial statements, copies of insurance policies, reinsurance agreements, and investment policy. Meeting required in domicile.

captive_administrator.name: Tolga Yalkin, CEO & Superintendent of Financial Institutions

regulator.name: BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA)
regulator.address: 600-750 West Pender Street, Vancouver, BC V6C 2T8

name: British Virgin Islands
summary: The BVI offers a seamless approach to captive formation, leveraging a long tenure in corporate domiciliation and a deep cadre of professional expertise. It licenses various captive categories, including Category E for pure captives and segregated portfolio companies that allow independent underwriting for owners. There is no corporate income tax in the BVI, and capital requirements vary based on the insurance line.
tax_notes: No corporate income tax

name: Cayman Islands
summary: The Cayman Islands is the world's second-largest captive domicile and the leading domicile for healthcare captives, regulated by the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority (CIMA) under the Insurance Act, 2010, as amended. International insurers are licensed as Class B (B(i) where at least 95 percent of net premiums come from related business, B(ii) where more than 50 percent are related, and B(iii) where 50 percent or less are related), Class C (fully collateralised insurance-linked structures) or Class D (open-market reinsurance). As of Q3 2026, CIMA reported 720 Class B, C and D insurers, writing US$62.3 billion of premium and holding US$202.9 billion of assets. Of that population, 337 were categorised as pure captives and 149 as group captives. Medical malpractice was the primary class of 127 licensees, and North America accounted for 632 licensees (88 percent). Class B segregated portfolio companies numbered 177, with 634 segregated portfolios and 68 portfolio insurance companies; those counts sit inside the 720 and are not additional licensees. In 2025 CIMA issued 42 international licences and cancelled 19. Through the 2026 year to date, issues and cancellations were 28 and 28, leaving the international total at 720. Every captive must appoint a licensed local insurance manager. CIMA states that a complete Class B or Class C application takes six to eight weeks. The Islands levy an annual licence fee rather than a premium tax, and CIMA describes the domicile as having no corporate or personal taxes.
legislation: Insurance Act, 2010 (Law 32 of 2010), as amended, and the Insurance (Capital and Solvency) (Classes B, C and D Insurers) Regulations (2018 Revision)
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act, 2010 (Law 32 of 2010), as amended, including the Insurance (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2024 (Act 14 of 2024); Insurance (Capital and Solvency) (Classes B, C and D Insurers) Regulations (2018 Revision); Insurance (Applications and Fees) Regulations (2026 Revision), as adjusted for Class B(i), (ii) and (iii) by the Insurance (Application and Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025, effective 1 January 2026; Insurance (Portfolio Insurance Companies) Regulations (2026 Revision); Companies Act (2026 Revision) segregated portfolio company provisions.

min_capital.Class B(i) General: US$100,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR
min_capital.Class B(i) Long-term: US$200,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR
min_capital.Class B(i) Composite: US$300,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR
min_capital.Class B(ii) General: US$150,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement is 10% of net earned premium on the first US$5 million, 5% on the next premium up to US$20 million, and 2.5% above US$20 million
min_capital.Class B(ii) Long-term: US$300,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR
min_capital.Class B(ii) Composite: US$450,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement is the general-business amount plus the MCR
min_capital.Class B(iii) General: US$200,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement is 15% of net earned premium on the first US$5 million, 7.5% on the next premium up to US$20 million, and 5% above US$20 million
min_capital.Class B(iii) Long-term: US$400,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR
min_capital.Class B(iii) Composite: US$600,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement is the general-business amount plus the MCR
min_capital.Class C (general, long-term, or composit: US$500 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR. Obligations must be fully collateralised. CIMA may set a higher requirement from the business plan
min_capital.Class D (open-market reinsurance): US$50,000,000 minimum capital requirement, with a risk-based prescribed capital requirement. The Authority may approve a reduced minimum in writing. This is not a captive class

tax_notes: No premium tax. The regulatory charge is a fixed annual licence fee under the Insurance (Applications and Fees) Regulations, as increased for Class B(i), (ii) and (iii) from 1 January 2026. CIMA states that the Cayman Islands is a tax-free domicile with no corporate or personal taxes.
contact_name: Kara Ebanks, Head of Insurance, Cayman Islands Monetary Authority
types_allowed: Class B(i) insurers (at least 95 percent related net premiums)
Class B(ii) insurers (more than 50 percent related net premiums)
Class B(iii) insurers (50 percent or less related net premiums)
Class C fully collateralised insurers and insurance-linked securities

fees.licensing_incorporation: Non-refundable application fee of CI$1,000 for a Class B, C or D insurer, plus a fee on the grant of the licence equal to the annual fee. Segregated portfolio companies pay an additional CI$1,000 application amount for each segregated portfolio. US-dollar payments use CIMA's published rate of US$1.00 = CI$0.82.
fees.annual_fees: Due 15 January. From 1 January 2026: Class B(i) CI$10,450 (US$12,743.90); Class B(ii) CI$11,550 (US$14,085.37); Class B(iii) CI$14,850 (US$18,109.76); Class C CI$6,500 (US$7,926.83); Class D CI$120,000 (US$146,341.46). An SPC pays an additional CI$1,000 a year for each segregated portfolio. A portfolio insurance company pays CI$1,000 a year. A penalty of one-twelfth of the annual fee accrues for each month the fee remains outstanding.
fees.premium_tax_rate: None. Regulatory cost is the fixed annual licence fee, not a percentage of premium.

annual_filing_requirements: Annual return within six months of financial year-end, including audited financial statements prepared to internationally recognised standards by a CIMA-approved auditor, and written confirmation that the licence information remains correct. An actuarial valuation and a solvency certification are also required, except that a Class C insurer or a Class B insurer that does not write long-term business does not have to file those two items. A Class B(iii) insurer must make its audited financial statements available to insured persons and third-party beneficiaries on request. Class B, C and D insurers also file a capital and solvency return by the prescribed filing date. Annual licence fees are due by 15 January.

captive_administrator.name: Kara Ebanks, Head of Insurance, Insurance Supervision Division, Cayman Islands Monetary Authority

licensing_speed: 6 to 8 weeks for a complete Class B or Class C application

regulator.name: Cayman Islands Monetary Authority, Insurance Supervision Division
regulator.address: Pavilion East, Cricket Square, 205 Elgin Avenue, PO Box 10052, Grand Cayman KY1-1001, Cayman Islands

name: China
summary: China's captive sector is primarily focused on pure captives owned by large state-owned or private enterprises with assets exceeding RMB 100 billion. The CBIRC oversees the industry, utilizing the China Risk Oriented Solvency System (C-ROSS) without exemption for captives. There are no specific tax exemptions for captives; they are subject to standard corporate tax rates of 25% and 6% VAT.
tax_notes: 25% Corporate tax; 6% VAT

name: Connecticut
summary: Connecticut, the 'insurance capital of the world,' has modernized its captive laws and application process to offer quick decisions and a risk-based regulatory approach. The state is unique for its concentration of insurtech, commercial insurers, and experienced regulators. It offers first-year premium tax credits of $7,500 and avoids the use of outside consultants to keep formation costs low.
tax_notes: $7,500 minimum; $200,000 maximum tax

name: Cook Islands
summary: The Cook Islands enacted its Captive Insurance Act in 2013 to regulate business conducted both inside and outside its borders by international companies. As of January 2022, companies are subject to a 20% tax on worldwide income to comply with EU standards and avoid non-cooperative listing. Domicile requirements include audited annual accounts filed with the Financial Supervisory Commission.
tax_notes: 20% worldwide income tax (as of 2022)

name: Delaware
summary: Delaware is a top-tier global domicile known for a regulatory bureau with exceptionally high levels of professional expertise and qualifications. It was the first US state to offer same-day conditional licensing, allowing captives to begin operations while their permanent application is reviewed. The state caters to a wide variety of structures, including series captives and risk retention groups.
tax_notes: $5,000 minimum tax ($3,500 for series captives)

name: District of Columbia
summary: The District of Columbia features a progressive insurance code and a knowledgeable staff specializing in captives and risk retention groups. It offers competitive costs for financial examinations and does not require a local director, though at least one annual board meeting must be facilitated from the district. Examination cycles occur every five years but can be extended upon request.
tax_notes: Favorable examination costs compared to other domiciles

name: Dubai
summary: The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) is a leading hub for the MEASA region, connecting emerging markets with a proven judicial system and an English common law framework. Regulated by the independent DFSA, the domicile offers 100% digital onboarding and a 0% tax rate on corporate income guaranteed until 2054. It allows for pure, third-party, and association captives with case-by-case flexibility on capital structures.
tax_notes: 0% tax until 2054; waived commercial license fees

name: Federated States of Micronesia
summary: Micronesia enacted its captive law in 2006 specifically to provide Japanese corporations with a conveniently located domicile under a responsive regulatory environment. Captives are required to file audited financial statements that can be prepared under US or Japanese GAAP. Beyond a low 0.05% premium tax, captives also file a simple annual income tax return computed at 21% of net income.
tax_notes: 0.05% premium tax; 21% net income tax

name: Florida
summary: Florida's captive provisions were augmented in 2012 to further specify criteria for formation, capital, and licensure. The state's unique selling point is its relatively low capital requirements across its four main captive types: pure, industrial insured, special purpose, and reinsurance. Interested parties are directed to Chapter 628 of the Florida statutes for detailed variation in requirement by captive type.
tax_notes: Requires annual reporting compliance

name: France
summary: France is a growing challenger in the European market, applying Solvency II regulations to ensure high quality in shareholders and solvency. Domiciling in France allows direct captives to operate across Europe under the Freedom of Service principle. The regulator, ACPR, maintains a dedicated team for captive supervision and emphasizes solid governance structured around '4 eyes' principles.
tax_notes: Freedom of Service access across the EU

name: Georgia
summary: The Georgia Insurance Department provides a healthy regulatory environment for captives, supported by 2018 legislation that improved formation efficiency. Georgia's premium tax structure is tiered and provides for captives under common ownership to be taxed as a single entity. The state emphasizes superior customer service to help its 50+ active captives succeed.
tax_notes: Max tax of $100,000 per year; reinsurance tax may be waived

name: Germany
summary: While not a typical domicile, Germany attracts captives through compliance requirements and the efficiency of sharing staff with parent companies and in-house brokers. Operations are governed by Solvency II and Section 122 VAG, with BaFin withdrawing authorization if eligible funds fall below strict minimums. Minimum capital requirements are calculated based on EU Delegated Regulation 2015/35.
tax_notes: No specific tax exemptions reported

name: Gibraltar
summary: As an onshore domicile for over 50 years, Gibraltar offers captive owners direct access to the UK market under flexible EU-based laws. It features a low flat tax rate of 10% which has been in effect since 2010. While capital requirements can be more onerous than offshore locations, the domicile permits varied structures including protected cell companies and managing general agents.

min_capital.General: More onerous than offshore; varies by structure

tax_notes: 10% across the board tax rate

name: Guam
summary: Guam offers a unique geographical advantage for US-linked business in the Pacific and features 100% tax abatement and rebates for corporate and gross receipts taxes. Legislation enacted in 1996 and subsequent amendments provide an attractive environment for risk management headquarters. Capital and surplus can be held in cash or irrevocable letters of credit approved by the commissioner.
tax_notes: 100% tax rebates for commercial and captive companies

name: Guernsey
summary: Guernsey is a leading captive centre and the jurisdiction that pioneered the protected cell company. The Guernsey Financial Services Commission regulates insurers under the Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, using its own solvency rules rather than the EU Solvency II standard formula. At 31 December 2025 the Commission reported 196 non-cellular captives, after 8 additions and 9 surrenders in 2025, and 126 captive cells, after 13 additions and 9 surrenders. The wider international sector totalled 549 entities: 223 companies, 44 protected cell companies, 222 PCC cells excluding insurance-linked securities, 14 incorporated cell companies and 46 ICC cells. The latest financial totals, for 2024, were £29.70 billion of gross assets, £12.62 billion of net worth and £5.19 billion of premiums written by international insurers as a whole, not by captives alone. Captive (re)insurers are Category 5 licensees. The capital floor is £100,000 for general business and £250,000 for long-term business, and the captive prescribed capital requirement is calibrated at a 90 percent confidence level over 12 months. Company income tax is 0 percent on insurance income that is not domestic business and 10 percent on domestic insurance business. Reinsurance is outside the statutory definition of domestic business. The Commission can pre-authorise later protected-cell-company cells on a product or class basis once the company and its first cell are approved, most often for fully collateralised special purpose insurer cells. It does not publish a 48-hour licensing standard.
legislation: Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, and the Insurance Business (Solvency) Rules and Guidance, 2021
applicable_legislation: Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002; Insurance Managers and Insurance Intermediaries (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002; Insurance Business (Solvency) Rules and Guidance, 2021, including the 2024 amendment to the retail general-business capital floor; Insurance Business Rules and Guidance, 2021; Companies (Guernsey) Law, 2008 (Commission consent to incorporate a protected cell company or an incorporated cell company); Financial Services Commission (Fees and Administrative Penalties) Regulations, 2025; Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975 (company standard rate 0 percent and intermediate rate 10 percent).

min_capital.Category 5 captive, general business: £100,000 capital floor. Paid-up share capital must be at least the capital floor, and minimum shareholders' funds must be at least 75 percent of the capital floor. The minimum capital requirement cannot be below the capital floor. The prescribed capital requirement is set at a 90 percent confidence level over the next 12 months
min_capital.Category 5 captive, long-term business: £250,000 capital floor, with the same paid-up capital, shareholders' funds and 90 percent prescribed-capital tests
min_capital.Protected cell company that does not wri: The capital floor applies to the PCC as a whole. There is no separate capital floor for each cell or for the core. Each cell and the core has a notional minimum capital requirement calculated as if it were a stand-alone insurer, and the PCC minimum is the sum of those amounts, subject to the capital floor

tax_notes: Company standard rate of income tax is 0 percent. The 10 percent company intermediate rate applies to domestic insurance business, insurance intermediary business and insurance manager business. Insurance income that is not domestic business, including reinsurance (which the Insurance Business Law excludes from domestic business), is taxed at 0 percent. Income from Guernsey land and buildings is taxed at 20 percent. Insurance is an economic-substance category for accounting periods after 1 January 2019. There is no premium-tax rate on the GFSC insurance fee schedule; the regulatory charge is the licence fee.
types_allowed: Category 5 captive insurers and reinsurers, including single-parent and association captives
Category 6 insurers, including special purpose insurers and insurance-linked securities

fees.licensing_incorporation: Under the Financial Services Commission (Fees and Administrative Penalties) Regulations, 2025, as summarised by the GFSC: Category 5 captive insurer or reinsurer application fee £7,850 for a company, PCC core or ICC core. A Category 5 cell of a PCC or ICC is £2,520. A Category 6 special purpose insurer cell is £110. A pro-rata annual fee is invoiced when the licence is issued.
fees.annual_fees: Due 31 January for licences in effect on 1 January. Category 5 captive insurer or reinsurer, including a PCC core or ICC: £7,850. Category 5 cell: £2,520. Category 6 company: £7,725. Category 6 cell that is not a special purpose insurer: £2,520. Special purpose insurer cell: £110. Dormant cell: £205. Change of general representative: £600. Change of controller: £2,760.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium-tax rate is set on the GFSC fee schedule. Company income tax is 0 percent on non-domestic insurance income and 10 percent on domestic insurance business.

annual_filing_requirements: Licensed insurers must deposit an annual return with the Commission within four months beginning on the close of the financial year (Insurance Business Law, section 37). The return includes the regulatory solvency assessment. Each insurer must also complete an Own Risk and Solvency Assessment at least annually and submit the resulting Own Solvency Capital Assessment with the annual return. The general representative is responsible for filing. A late return attracts an administrative financial penalty. Licensed insurance managers and insurance intermediaries deposit their annual return within six months of the financial year-end. Guernsey company income tax returns are filed separately with the Revenue Service; the 2025 corporate return is due 30 November 2026.

captive_administrator.name: Guernsey Financial Services Commission, Banking and Insurance Division

licensing_speed: No published standard timeline. PCC cells may be pre-authorised on a product or class basis after the PCC and its first cell are approved; this route is most commonly used for fully collateralised special purpose insurer cells.

regulator.name: Guernsey Financial Services Commission
regulator.address: Regency Court, Glategny Esplanade, St Peter Port, Guernsey, GY1 3HQ

name: Hawaii
summary: With over 30 years of experience, Hawaii is a premier Pacific domicile recognized for its partnership-based approach with captive owners. The insurance commissioner guides capital requirements based on individual programs across five license classes. Taxes are limited to a $200,000 maximum, and there is no taxation on reinsurance premiums assumed by a captive.
tax_notes: Max premium tax $200,000; tiered rates

name: Hong Kong
summary: Hong Kong is a leading Asian financial hub that encourages captive establishment through simple tax regimes and targeted concessions for marine and specialty insurance. Since 2013, it has provided a 50% reduction in corporate tax for offshore business, later extended to onshore risks. The Insurance Authority's strategic vision is to build a regional hub through a bespoke regime for insurance-linked securities (ILS).
tax_notes: 16.5% Corporate tax; 50% concession available

name: Illinois
summary: Illinois modernized its Insurance Code in 2018 to lower capital and surplus requirements and filing fees, making the state a more viable captive domicile. The state now allows captives to make loans to affiliates with prior approval and permits captive reinsurance pools. Despite having one of the highest GDPs in the US, Illinois has only recently become an active competitor in the captive space.
tax_notes: $2,000 filing fee (lowered from $7,000)

name: Ireland
summary: Ireland is a global re/insurance center that provides a stable operating environment with direct access to all EEA countries through EU passporting. The Central Bank of Ireland (CBI) applies Solvency II proportionately through its PRISM system, which allows captives to have fewer directors and less frequent meetings. The state is also known for managing non-traditional risks like employee benefits.

min_capital.Requirement: Adheres to EU Solvency II framework

tax_notes: Transparent tax regime; Freedom of Service (FoS) access

name: Isle of Man
summary: The Isle of Man offers proportional capital requirements and a pragmatic regulatory environment with a strong Moody's Aa3 rating. It is distinguished by bespoke legislation for catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities. A key flexibility is the ability for captives to provide a loan back to their parent company.
tax_notes: GBP 6,694 annual standalone charge

name: Jersey
summary: Jersey has a growing reputation as an alternative location that follows international IAIS standards rather than Solvency II. The market has grown by over 30% in recent years due to an 'open for business' approach and the capability to handle both long and short-term risks. The JFSC maintains the discretion to amend capital requirements based on business projections.
tax_notes: Solvency margin at 17.5% of net premium for general business

name: Kansas
summary: Kansas law provides for pure, association, branch, and special purpose captives, with specific reporting requirements due by March 1 each year. Association captives can utilize letters of credit from state-chartered banks for capital requirements. The domicile leverages the NAIC Uniform Certificate of Authority for admission documents.
tax_notes: Tax paid on all premiums received on risks in the state

name: Kazakhstan
summary: The Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) is a unique hub that offers incentives to attract Kazakhstani capital and assets back from foreign jurisdictions. It provides three captive classes and utilizes a specific formula to calculate the premium risk component of capital. The jurisdiction is noted for its relocation-friendly regime, exemplified by the move of the Kazakhstan Energy Reinsurance Company from Bermuda.
legislation: AIFC Insurance and Reinsurance Prudential Rules
tax_notes: Friendly tax regime and operational incentives

name: Kentucky
summary: Kentucky is an established midwestern domicile that has grown to over 80 licensed captives across diverse industries like healthcare, banking, and manufacturing. It features a dedicated staff and graduated premium tax rates that become lower as premium volumes rise. A minimum annual tax of $5,000 is required if regular premium taxes fall below that threshold.
tax_notes: $5,000 minimum annual premium tax

name: Labuan
summary: Labuan IBFC is Asia's premier international financial hub, uniquely offering shariah-compliant Islamic captives, known as takaful captives. It is a substance-enabling jurisdiction with access to Malaysia's network of over 70 double taxation treaties. Every captive must have an operational office in Labuan or appoint a licensed underwriting manager.
legislation: Labuan Islamic Financial Services and Securities Act 2010

min_capital.Requirement: Risk-commensurate working funds in a Labuan bank

tax_notes: Fiscal neutrality and certainty

name: Liechtenstein
summary: Liechtenstein offers an adept workforce and unique central European access to both the EU and Switzerland markets. Captives are subject to Solvency II and can insure subsidiaries across the European Economic Area and third countries. While it does not tax capital, it applies a flat 12.5% tax rate on taxable income.
tax_notes: 12.5% flat tax on income; CHF 30,000 license fee

name: Luxembourg
summary: Luxembourg is the largest captive reinsurance domicile in the EU, attracting global firms with its stable democracy and modern legal framework. It allows captives with low risk diversification to build large technical reserves for high-risk, low-frequency exposures. The minister must authorize a local manager for all reinsurance activities established in the state.
tax_notes: Secure legal and tax framework; infrastructure-rich

name: Malta
summary: Malta is the only EU member state with protected cell company (PCC) legislation that extends to brokers and insurance managers beyond traditional insurers. Its PCCs offer unique shared economies of scale and direct access to the EU market, effectively reducing fronting costs. The domicile is Fitch A+ rated and focuses on facilitating blockchain technology and legal certainty for smart contracts.
tax_notes: Direct access to UK and EU markets

name: Mauritius
summary: Mauritius is an emerging African domicile that provides stability with no exchange controls and an innovative pool of financial products. New proposed rules distinguish four classes of captive business based on the percentage of gross written premium originating from affiliates. Minimum unimpaired paid-up capital starts at approximately $86,750 for pure captives.
tax_notes: Long-standing bilateral relations with Africa

name: Michigan
summary: Michigan licenses a wide range of captives, including non-profit pure and special purpose financial captives. It maintains a strict resident requirement where two out of three organizers must be state residents, and board meetings must be held in-state. Notably, the state does not have a premium tax rate, using a renewal fee based on premium volume instead.
tax_notes: No tax rate; premium-volume based renewal fee

name: Missouri
summary: Centrally located with major non-stop flight access, Missouri emphasizes cost-reduction by using expert in-house analysts rather than outside consultants. It licenses varied structures, including special purpose life and sponsored cell captives. Application and licensing fees are deductible, helping to lower the barrier for new formations.
tax_notes: Direct tax rates tiered (0.38% down to 0.072%)

name: Montana
summary: Montana is recognized for having accessible regulators and one of the few regimes that offers special purpose captives under a series limited liability structure. This allows smaller captives to form with capital based on premium writing rather than a fixed minimum. The state legislature is extremely supportive, and captives are subject to mandatory examination at least every five years.
tax_notes: $5,000 minimum; $100,000 maximum tax

name: Netherlands
summary: The Dutch regulator, De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB), offers a robust supervision framework and has a deep understanding of captive-specific characteristics. Popular with Asian and American holding companies, the domicile has a local community of owners that evaluate supervisory topics. It is home to both insurance and reinsurance captives and features an exceptionally well-educated, English-speaking workforce.
tax_notes: Robust supervision framework

name: Nevada
summary: Nevada is one of the oldest US domiciles and frequently ranks first in new business launches due to its lack of corporate or personal income taxes. In 2019, it added a dormant captive status, allowing inactive companies to retain their certificate with fewer compliance requirements. Examination fees were also recently reduced by 33% to remain competitive.
tax_notes: $175,000 maximum tax; first-year credit up to $5,000

name: Nevis
summary: Nevis has provided a well-regulated international jurisdiction since 2004, geared toward the long-term viability of captives. It offers a low-cost environment with no tax on premiums, assets, or net income. Captives are formed as corporations but have a 'menu' of legal ownership options including trusts and LLCs to align with parent structures.
tax_notes: No tax paid on premiums, income, or assets

name: New Jersey
summary: New Jersey is an accessible domicile for Fortune 500 companies, regulated by the DOBI commissioner who actively seeks to modernize the market. The state enacted its legislation in 2011 and requires captives to hold at least one board meeting in the state per year. The commissioner holds discretionary authority to increase capital requirements based on the volume and nature of insurance.
tax_notes: $200,000 maximum annual tax

name: New Zealand
summary: New Zealand does not have specific captive-only legislation, instead governing all insurance through the IPSA 2010 act. Captives are explicitly exempt from the financial strength rating requirements that apply to traditional insurers. To obtain a license, a captive must demonstrate 'fitness for business' and the capacity to manage its specific risks.
tax_notes: Captives with no NZ business may fall outside IPSA scope

name: North Carolina
summary: North Carolina has rapidly achieved prominence due to its modern law and an in-house regulatory team focused on accessibility and customer service. It utilizes a secure online filing system to streamline the application process. The commissioner maintains discretion to allow lower capital amounts if a feasibility study proves adequacy.
tax_notes: $100,000 maximum tax ($200,000 for cells with >10 cells)

name: Oklahoma
summary: Oklahoma is recognized for continuous innovation, offering competitive arrays of investment options and a provisional license for new applicants and redomestications. In 2020, it introduced an incentive for 'Series' captives to maintain only $50,000 in capital if certain risk-segregation criteria are met. Captives are permitted to conduct a broad selection of coverages, including workers' compensation.
tax_notes: 0.2% direct / 0.1% assumed rates; $100,000 cap

name: Oregon
summary: Oregon describes itself as a business-friendly domicile that collaboratively forms captives for financial success and legal compliance. A notable attribute is that Oregon does not collect any premium tax, charging only a flat initial and annual renewal fee. All captives are examined at least once every three years by the Division of Financial Regulation.
tax_notes: No premium tax; $5,000 annual renewal fee

name: Panama
summary: Captive insurance in Panama is subject to Law 60 of 1996, which distinguishes between long-term life risks and general risks. In Panama, local risks are generally not insurable; the law focuses on foreign risks managed from a physically identified office in Panama. Obtaining a license is a two-stage process involving legal vehicle registration followed by a superintendent license request.
tax_notes: $2,000 annual service fee

name: Puerto Rico
summary: Puerto Rico offers a unique 'dual sovereignty' environment, governed by standard US federal oversight while Puerto Rican law takes precedence in corporate and insurance matters. It maintains an International Insurance Center as a one-stop regulatory shop for over 450 active captives. Pure captives utilize a 5:1 premium to surplus ratio, while association captives cap third-party risks at 20%.
tax_notes: Preferred tax environment; Class-based application fees

name: Singapore
summary: After licensing its first captive in 1983, Singapore has grown into the largest Asia Pacific captive domicile and a major reinsurance center. It is governed by the Insurance Act and offers chargeable income tax exemptions of up to SGD 152,500. Capital adequacy is set strictly such that equity and retained earnings must exceed the sum of SGD 400,000 and calculated insurance fund components.
tax_notes: 17% corporate rate with 10% concessionary rate for qualifying activity

name: South Carolina
summary: South Carolina is the only mature domicile in the southeastern US, featuring 22 years of operation and a savvy regulatory environment. It focuses on owner value across structures like risk retention groups and special purpose financial captives. The state is recognized for its business-friendly climate and world-class captive know-how.
tax_notes: Tiered direct rates (0.4% down to set $100k blocks)

name: South Dakota
summary: South Dakota is nationally recognized for user-friendly trust laws and a common-sense regulatory environment where owners work directly with decision makers. It does not charge premium taxes, opting instead for a supervision fee that can never exceed $50,000 annually. Captives must maintain their principal place of business and hold at least one board meeting in the state with a physical quorum.
tax_notes: No premium tax; supervision fee capped at $50,000

name: St Lucia
summary: St Lucia requires all insurance applications to be conducted through an international business company (IBC) with a local registered agent and office. The FSRA maintains the discretion to fix solvency margins and guidelines distinguish between Class A, B, and C licenses based on risk type. IBC structures generally enjoy tax-neutral status unless they elect for a 1% tax.
tax_notes: No tax unless 1% election is made; special confidentiality provisions

name: Switzerland
summary: Switzerland boasts top-tier political and fiscal stability, with major insurance hubs in Zurich and Zug offering a vast pool of experienced staff. Captives benefit from proportional regulation and relief from tied-asset regulations for intra-group activities. The Swiss Solvency Test (SST) is basically parallel to EU requirements, offering simplified models for reinsurance captives.

min_capital.Requirement: FINMA prescribed; takes less than one year to comply

tax_notes: OECD compliant tax levels; many cantons have lowered corporate tax

name: Tennessee
summary: Tennessee was one of the first onshore US domiciles and has grown to rank in the top 20 globally after modernizing its statute in 2011. It is one of the few states that allows series limited liability companies, offering lower administrative burdens for incorporated cells. The state even offers a one-year tax holiday for alien captives redomesticating to Tennessee.
tax_notes: $5,000 minimum tax; tiered rates with $100,000 max

name: Texas
summary: Texas focuses on single-parent captives to help business owners protect the enterprise value they create. While primarily supportive of single-parent structures, the state seeks to create the most broadly constructive statute possible for this category. The Texas Department of Insurance examines actuarial projections and other issues before finalizing any formation decisions.
tax_notes: 0.5% premium tax; $7,500 min / $200,000 max

name: The Bahamas
summary: The Bahamas licenses captives as restricted external insurers under the External Insurance Act, 2009 (Chapter 348), supervised by the Insurance Commission of The Bahamas. A restricted external insurer may cover its members, subsidiaries and affiliates, reinsureds who acknowledge in writing that it is restricted, and other persons the Commission approves. Unrestricted external insurers may write broader business from The Bahamas. Cell programmes use segregated accounts companies under the Segregated Accounts Companies Act (Chapter 369C). The Commission does not publish a current captive or external-insurer census; the statistics page covers domestic general and long-term business, and the latest files there run through 2022. Capital for a restricted insurer is the amount the Commission approves. The prescribed floors for unrestricted insurers are B$100,000 for general business, B$200,000 for long-term business and B$300,000 for both. The annual licence fee is B$2,500 for a restricted insurer and B$3,500 for an unrestricted insurer. Section 52 of the Act gives a licensed external insurer a 20-year exemption, running from the date of its first licence, from Bahamian taxes, fees, duties and imposts other than provisions of that kind already in force when the Act commenced and other than licence charges under the Act. Audited financial statements are due within four months of the financial year-end. The Commission has posted a Draft External Insurance Act, 2025; this profile follows the 2009 Act and the 2010 regulations.
legislation: External Insurance Act, 2009 (Chapter 348) and the External Insurance Regulations, 2010
applicable_legislation: External Insurance Act, 2009 (Chapter 348); External Insurance (Capital Requirements for External Insurers, Insurance Managers and External Insurance Brokers) Regulations, 2010; External Insurance (Forms and Fees) Regulations, 2010; External Insurance (Classes of Insurance Business) Regulations, 2010; External Insurance (Variable Insurance Business) Regulations, 2010; Segregated Accounts Companies Act (Chapter 369C). The Insurance Commission also publishes a Draft External Insurance Act, 2025, which is not treated as in force here.

min_capital.Restricted external insurer (captive): Paid-up capital or contributed reserve in the amount approved by the Commission, in cash or other approved assets (External Insurance Act, 2009, s.22(2))
min_capital.Unrestricted external insurer, general b: B$100,000 minimum fully paid-up capital, capital surplus and subordinated capital or contributed reserve fund
min_capital.Unrestricted external insurer, long-term: B$200,000 minimum fully paid-up capital, capital surplus and subordinated capital or contributed reserve fund
min_capital.Unrestricted external insurer, general a: B$300,000 minimum fully paid-up capital, capital surplus and subordinated capital or contributed reserve fund
min_capital.Solvency, restricted general insurer: Assets must exceed liabilities by the amount the Commission prescribes (s.31(2))
min_capital.Solvency, unrestricted general insurer: After the first financial year, assets must exceed liabilities by one-fifth of the preceding year's premium income where that income does not exceed B$5 million; where premium income exceeded B$5 million, by B$1 million plus one-tenth of the amount by which premium income exceeded B$10 million, unless the Commission determines otherwise (s.31(1))

tax_notes: The External Insurance Act does not impose a premium tax. Section 52 exempts a licensed external insurer, for 20 years from the date of its first licence, from any tax, fee, duty or impost in The Bahamas, other than provisions of that kind in force when the Act commenced and other than amounts payable for a licence under the Act. The standing annual charge is the licence fee.

fees.licensing_incorporation: B$250 application for an external insurer licence; B$250 application for a segregated account of an external insurer; B$100 application for an insurance manager or external insurance broker. The application fee is not repaid if a licence is refused (External Insurance Act, s.8(3), and the 2010 Forms and Fees Regulations, Sixth Schedule).
fees.annual_fees: Restricted external insurer B$2,500; unrestricted external insurer B$3,500; insurance manager B$1,000; external insurance broker B$1,000. Late payment adds 10, 15, 20 or 25 percent of the amount due, according to the quarterly ageing of the overdue fee.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax under the External Insurance Act. Section 52 provides a 20-year exemption from other Bahamian taxes, fees, duties and imposts, subject to the carve-outs in that section. The annual regulatory charge is the licence fee above.

annual_filing_requirements: Audited financial statements, complying with international accounting standards or another standard the Commission determines, are due within four months after the financial year-end, or any longer period the Commission allows. They must be audited by a Commission-approved auditor and accompanied by the auditor's report and by the auditor's certificate on the statutory books, compliance with the section 31 solvency test at the balance-sheet date, and compliance with anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing reporting. The Commission may also require an actuary's certificate that reserves are adequate. A licensee whose outstanding claims, including incurred-but-not-reported claims, exceed 200 percent of capital and surplus must file an annual actuarial review of those claims. A licensee incorporated outside The Bahamas must, within four months of year-end, file a certificate from its overseas regulator. Each licensee must maintain a resident representative in The Bahamas. The external-insurer licence is renewable annually.

captive_administrator.name: Dana Munnings-Gray, Superintendent of Insurance, Insurance Commission of The Bahamas

regulator.name: Insurance Commission of The Bahamas
regulator.address: Silk Cotton House, Prospect Ridge Road, P.O. Box N-4844, Nassau, New Providence, The Bahamas

name: Turks and Caicos Islands
summary: As a UK overseas territory, Turks and Caicos uses a British common law legal framework and is tax neutral, with no income or corporate taxes. Incorporation can be achieved within two days, and an insurance license can normally be obtained within 10 business days for well-prepared applications. Both pure captives and producer-owned reinsurance companies (PORCs) are welcomed.

min_capital.Requirement: Varies by amount of capitalization and application queries

tax_notes: No local sales, income, or corporation taxes

name: US Virgin Islands
summary: The US Virgin Islands is an emerging market positioned to capture small and medium-sized captives by offering the lowest minimum capital and surplus requirements in the industry. Its legislation covers varied structures, including industrial insured and special purpose financial captives. It also features the lowest registration fees, set at 5% of qualified manager net revenues.
legislation: Title 22, Chapters 55 and 66, Virgin Islands Code
tax_notes: 5% of qualified manager net revenues for registration/annual fees

name: Utah
summary: Utah is a leading domicile for technological advancement, handling all annual filings and applications via a smooth online portal. A major selling point is that Utah does not impose any state or premium taxes, charging only a flat annual fee. Recent statutory amendments allow captives to cover punitive damages, provided they do not arise from criminal acts.
tax_notes: No premium or state tax; flat annual fee of $6,375

name: Vanuatu
summary: Vanuatu is a full-service financial center regulated by the Reserve Bank of Vanuatu, offering easy repatriation for existing captives from other jurisdictions. The regulatory framework is flexible and mirrors other well-regulated jurisdictions in its reporting and capital systems. While directors do not need to be local, the captive must appoint a resident insurance manager and auditor.
tax_notes: $250 application fee; $2,000 annual license fee

name: Vermont
summary: Vermont is the largest onshore captive domicile in the United States and a premier global captive hub, having pioneered the US industry with the enactment of the Special Insurer Act of 1981 (8 V.S.A. Chapter 141). Regulated by the Vermont Department of Financial Regulation (DFR) Captive Insurance Division—which maintains a dedicated in-house team of analysts and financial examiners—and supported by the Vermont Captive Insurance Association (VCIA), the state had 707 licensed captives ($243.6B in assets and $36.3B in gross written premium) at year-end 2025. Vermont licenses nine distinct captive structures, offers a 30-day licensing turnaround, and provides a competitive graduated premium tax capped at $200,000 with a $5,000 tax credit in each of the first two years.
legislation: Special Insurer Act of 1981 (Title 8 V.S.A. Chapters 141, 142, and 142A)
applicable_legislation: Title 8, Vermont Statutes Annotated (V.S.A.), Chapter 141 (Captive Insurance Companies, 8 V.S.A. §§ 6001–6049o), Chapter 142 (Risk Retention Groups and Purchasing Groups), and Chapter 142A (Risk Retention Group Managing General Agents, Reinsurance Intermediaries, and Producer Controlled Insurers); Vermont DFR Regulation C-81-2 (Captive Insurance Financial Regulation).
tax_notes: Graduated direct premium tax (0.38% on first $20M, 0.285% on next $20M, 0.19% on next $20M, 0.072% over $60M) and assumed reinsurance tax (0.214% on first $20M, 0.143% on next $20M, 0.048% on next $20M, 0.024% over $60M); $7,500 minimum and $200,000 maximum annual cap; $5,000 tax credit in each of the first 2 years; no Vermont corporate income tax on captives.
contact_name: Christine Brown, Deputy Commissioner of Captive Insurance
types_allowed: Sponsored cell captives (Protected and Incorporated cells)

fees.licensing_incorporation: USD $500 initial licensure fee (USD $5,000 for SPFI) plus USD $6,000 actuarial application review fee (USD $10,000 for SPFI).
fees.annual_fees: USD $500 annual license renewal fee due April 1 (USD $5,000 for SPFI).
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums: 0.38% on first $20M, 0.285% on next $20M, 0.19% on next $20M, 0.072% over $60M. Assumed reinsurance premiums: 0.214% on first $20M, 0.143% on next $20M, 0.048% on next $20M, 0.024% over $60M. Minimum annual tax: $7,500; Maximum annual tax cap: $200,000 (consolidated cap for sponsored captives and common ownership groups). $5,000 tax credit in each of the first 2 years.

annual_filing_requirements: Annual financial report (VCAR or NAIC statement) due by March 15 for pure, association, sponsored, industrial insured, and agency captives, and by March 1 for RRGs and other captives (or within 75 days of fiscal year-end if approved for an alternative fiscal year). Annual audited financial statements and actuarial opinion due by June 30 (or 6 months after fiscal year-end). Board of directors (or committee of managers) must hold at least one annual meeting in Vermont.

captive_administrator.name: Christine Brown, Deputy Commissioner of Captive Insurance

regulator.name: Vermont Department of Financial Regulation (DFR), Captive Insurance Division

name: Virginia
summary: Virginia law permits both stock and non-stock captive incorporations, with non-stock entities requiring a higher $4 million surplus. Association captives must demonstrate that they have been in existence for at least one year, unless each member contributes over $100,000 in gross annual premium. Pure captives are required to show aggregate annual premiums of at least $500,000.
tax_notes: 2.25% premium tax rate on gross written premiums
